Section 8—
19

One of the most significant differences between the 1827 Illinois statute and the 1842 Nauvoo ordinance was the Nauvoo ordinance’s omission of section 8 of the Illinois statute. This section acknowledged the supremacy of federal courts and stated that the state courts could not issue writs of habeas corpus for prisoners in federal custody. Specifically mentioned were prisoners of war, those awaiting extradition for high crimes such as treason, and slaves. While states like Illinois and New York explicitly acknowledged the supremacy of federal jurisdiction for habeas corpus, many other states claimed that their state courts held “concurrent jurisdiction” with federal courts. The omission of this section suggests that the city council was theoretically attempting to place Nauvoo’s municipal court on a level with state or federal courts in matters of habeas corpus. (See An Act . . . on Writs of Habeas Corpus, p. 325, sec. 8; and Kent, Commentaries on American Law, 1:375–376.)

Kent, James. Commentaries on American Law. Vol. 2. New York: O. Halsted, 1827.

21

Section 9 of the 1827 statute allowed state courts to delay habeas corpus proceedings under certain conditions to give sufficient time to procure evidence. The passages here loosely adapted those instructions for the municipal court, though the Nauvoo ordinance focused more explicitly on gathering witnesses and testimony. Additionally, the Nauvoo ordinance included a thirty-day deadline to decide the case. (An Act . . . on Writs of Habeas Corpus, pp. 325–326, sec. 9.)

22

Nauvoo’s city ordinance omitted section 10 of the 1827 statute. This section forbade moving prisoners on a habeas corpus writ within fifteen days of the next term of the circuit court of that jurisdiction. (An Act . . . on Writs of Habeas Corpus, p. 326, sec. 10.)
